content: Here’s the latest twist on FTC impersonators: someone claiming to be an FTC official (who’s really a scammer) calls to say a phone was registered under your name and number and is being used to commit scams in another country. The “FTC official” even reads off their badge ID (it’s a fake badge). If you don’t cooperate, they threaten to deactivate your phone number. Sounds scary? That’s (unfortunately) the point. To keep making the story sound real, the FTC impersonator will transfer you to a (fake) police officer to file a report. If you hesitate, they might have you call back the police department directly. They’ll tell you what to search online to find the number. It feels like you’re verifying the story, but it’s all part of their scheme. And when you call, people involved in the scam pick up. They ask for your ID and other personal information for your “report” and tell you to keep everything secret. Later, you get more bad news: They claim you’re under arrest for the scams your phone number was associated with — and they say you have to go to another country. Unless you send money for a security deposit. None of this is true — it’s all a scam. A real FTC employee will never ever reach out to ask you to send money, and will never connect you to someone who says to send money. That’s a scam. A real FTC employee will never ever threaten to disconnect your phone. That’s a scam. A real FTC employee will never ever tell you to keep your conversations secret. That’s always a scam. A real FTC employee will never ever text you a photo of their employee ID to “verify” their identity. Learn more about how to spot and avoid scammers who pretend to be from the government. Spot one of these scams? Tell the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

content: If you’re thinking of buying a franchise, you’re probably considering lots of factors — weighing benefits like training and brand name recognition with potential risks and costs. Like any other business, a franchise has no guarantee of success. That’s why franchisors are required to give potential buyers honest information about what it takes to open and operate their franchise. The Franchise Disclosure Document (FDD) has important details about upfront and ongoing costs, market competition, and the franchisor’s litigation and bankruptcy history. When information in the FDD isn’t complete or accurate, it can cost prospective buyers — small business owners — their hard-earned (and sometimes life) savings. According to the FTC, that’s what happened to more than 200 people, including veterans, who paid to open Premier Martial Arts franchises. The FTC charged the franchisor with misrepresenting potential earnings and making other claims that weren’t accurate or supported by the FDD — for example, that non-martial artists could profitably run their franchises working less than 15 hours a week. So if you’re considering buying a franchise, here are some things to know: Franchisors aren’t required to provide sales or earnings information, but many do. Any claims a franchise seller makes about sales, income, or profits must be in Item 19 of the FDD. Franchisors must be honest about how much you’re likely to earn when you buy a franchise, and any information they provide in the FDD must be complete and accurate. The franchisor is required to give you substantiation if you ask. So ask the franchisor for written substantiation that supports the claims they make. An accountant or lawyer can help you determine whether the claims are reasonable. Franchisors must provide contact information for current and former franchisees. Talking to them may help you assess the franchisor’s claims and provide additional information that may not be included in the FDD. Reach out to as many of them as possible (here are some questions you can ask). For more, check out A Consumer’s Guide to Buying a Franchise.

content: Sextortion — when someone threatens to share your intimate images unless you pay — can be stressful and upsetting. And figuring out what to do can be overwhelming. While searching for help, you might find companies that offer quick fixes (for a price) but don’t deliver on their promises. One example, according to the lawsuit filed by the FTC, is Digital Forensics, a company behind websites like BlackmailHelpline.com, DigitalForensics.com, CyberBlackmail911.com, and SecurityBreach911.com. The FTC alleges that Digital Forensics falsely promised to stop sextortion threats, prevent explicit material from spreading online, and report the perpetrators to criminal authorities. They charged customers thousands of dollars and failed to deliver on their promises — adding a big financial burden to an already stressful ordeal. So, what can you do about threats of sextortion? Ignore and block the blackmailer. Don’t pay them or give them access to your devices or financial accounts. Ignore their messages and stop communicating with them. Talk with someone you trust. Like a trusted friend, family member, or counselor and tell them what’s going on. Report them to criminal law enforcement. Sextortion is a serious crime. Report the perpetrator to your local police and to the FBI ( fbi.gov, 1-800-225-5324). If it involves a minor, report it through the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children’s CyberTipline. Here’s what to know and do if someone shared your intimate images without your permission: Report it directly to the platform. The Take It Down Act requires online platforms to remove intimate images within 48 hours of your request — for free. If the platform doesn’t take it down within 48 hours, report it to the FTC at TakeItDown.ftc.gov. Research paid services carefully. If a company claims to help you remove the intimate images for a fee, check it out first. Search online for the company name with words like “scam,” “review,” or “complaint.” And scroll past the paid search results. Get free counseling and support services. Minors, contact the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (1-800-843-5678). Adults, contact the National Domestic Violence Hotline (1-800-799-7233).

content: Did someone share an explicit image of your child online? Possessing or sharing explicit images of children can be a serious crime — and that includes AI-generated deepfakes. Report the perpetrator immediately to criminal law enforcement and take action to get online platforms to remove the images as quickly as possible. Report the incident to the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children’s (NCMEC’s) CyberTipline, or call 1-800-843-5678. NCMEC’s trained analysts make your report available to the appropriate law enforcement agency. Contact the FBI directly by calling 1-800-CALL-FBI, or visit a local FBI field office. Request removal and help stop the spread Tell the platform to take down the image. The Take It Down Act requires covered platforms to give parents an easy way to request the removal of explicit images of a child. If you have an account with the platform, log in and use the report option, which may be on or near the image — often, this option is in the three dots you’ll see in the upper right corner of the image. If you don't have an account with the platform, check the platform's help center for removal request instructions. Report a platform that fails to remove the explicit image. If the covered platform doesn’t take down the image within 48 hours, report them to the FTC at TakeItDown.ftc.gov. Help prevent the image from being shared elsewhere online. Use NCMEC’s Take It Down service which creates a hash, like a digital fingerprint of the image, to help suppress it from appearing in other places online. Taking these steps can help protect your child and limit the harm. Learn more at TakeItDown.ftc.gov, where you’ll find links to support and guidance. Acting quickly can make a meaningful difference.

content: Kids face a lot of challenges online: from cyberbullying and scams to digitally altered deepfakes, like nudify apps that create fake nude photos and videos of real people. Even if you’ve had conversations with your child about online safety and sensitive topics like deepfakes, you probably know parents who are concerned about these topics, too. If so, consider using the FTC resources below to help you learn more and share with fellow parents. Kids and teens don’t always recognize the risks of sharing explicit images or deepfakes, even as a joke. But fake explicit images of children posted online cause real harm. That’s why the Take It Down Act requires covered platforms — like social media, messaging, and photo or video sharing apps — to give you a way to request the removal of an explicit photo or video of your child, including deepfakes. The law says platforms must remove the image, and known identical copies, within 48 hours of your request. Visit TakeItDown.ftc.gov to learn more. If you’re talking about online safety basics with your child — things like respecting other people's boundaries and asking before sharing anything about someone online — pass along this advice: Don’t share explicit images or deepfakes, even as a joke. Possessing or sharing explicit images of children can be a serious crime. Say no to anyone who asks for an explicit picture, video, or “nudes.” Talk to a parent or trusted adult if you see an explicit photo or video of yourself or someone you know online. Did someone share, or threaten to share, an explicit photo or video of your child online? Visit TakeItDown.ftc.gov.

content: Health insurance scams happen year-round, but they pick up during Open Enrollment for Medicare and the Marketplace. If you’re looking to find a new plan, you might search online. For additional help with ACA plans, visit HealthCare.gov and click “Find Local Help.” Learn more. Join a roundtable conversation about Medicare and healthcare-related scams with representatives from the FTC, Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, and the Senior Medicare Patrol on September 29, 2026 at 1pm ET. content: The FTC is hearing about a scam targeting some of the hardest working people out there: farmers. Scammers posing as farm equipment businesses are selling (fake) equipment to farmers, who end up empty-handed. Here’s how the scam works and how to avoid it. It starts like this: you might scroll through social media and see an ad for a tractor. It’s a good price and looks like it’s from a legit business. Or you search online and see a tractor from a business you know, and maybe even bought equipment from before.  In either case, when you contact them, they send a purchase agreement and invoice. They typically ask you to send thousands of dollars — usually by wire transfer — as a deposit or full payment, and schedule a delivery date. What happens next? The delivery never comes. It turns out this was never a legit business and was all a scam. The scammer either stops answering or makes up another excuse (e.g., there’s an issue with the delivery truck). You’re out both the money and a tractor. How can you (or your local farmer) avoid these and other impersonation scams? Before you buy based on any ad, check it out. Social media companies don’t always vet ads. Do some research by searching online for the company name plus “scam” or “complaint.” Know that the first search results you see might be paid ads. Sometimes scammers place them: they pretend to be a real business but use their own contact info instead. Scroll past those ads to the unpaid search results to help confirm you have the right website or contact information. Never send money to anyone who says you can only pay by wire transfer, gift card, cryptocurrency, or payment app. Scammers prefer these methods because once they’ve collected the money, it’s almost impossible to get it back. Spot an impersonation scam? Tell the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

content: Did someone violate your trust and privacy by sharing your intimate images online without your consent? Or did they digitally alter or create an intimate image of you? You have rights — and online platforms have obligations to help. You may know that websites and social media platforms that host user-generated content let you report content that violates their community guidelines. But did you know that platforms covered by the Take It Down Act are legally required to give you a way to report intimate images shared without your consent — including deepfakes? And that platforms must take down the images (and copies of the images) within 48 hours? If you discover that someone shared intimate images of you without your permission: Report the image directly to the platform. Report it from the post or image: Find the post where the intimate image was shared and look for an option to report the content. You might find it by tapping the three dots in the upper right corner of the post. Report it through the platform’s support pages: Use the platform’s help or support features or look up contact information for the platform in this directory from StopNCII.org. Take action to stop the photo or video from spreading online. Visit StopNCII.org, a free global tool operated by the Revenge Porn Helpline and select “Create Your Case.” Select the image from your phone, tablet, or computer. StopNCII.org creates a “digital fingerprint” of the image and shares the fingerprint (not the image) with participating platforms. Platforms scan for matches and block the image from being posted online. What if the platform doesn’t remove the nonconsensual intimate image? The Take It Down Act requires online platforms to remove intimate photos or videos within 48 hours of your request. If the platform doesn’t take it down within 48 hours, report it to the FTC at TakeItDown.ftc.gov.

content: Recent violent storms, tornadoes, wildfires, heat waves, and extreme flooding are a reminder that severe weather and natural disasters can happen anytime, anywhere, and with little warning. September is National Preparedness Month and it’s a great time to plan for whatever may come your way. Scammers are always looking for ways to steal people’s money and personal information. Use the FTC’s site, Dealing with Weather Emergencies, to help prepare for a weather emergency — while avoiding the scams that often follow. To stay ahead of weather-related scams, get started now with these steps. Check your insurance. Find out if any of your home, health, or other insurance policies will pay for temporary shelter, replacement clothing, furniture, or other items if you are affected by extreme weather or a disaster. Organize important papers. Scan and upload PDFs of important documents to personal cloud storage. Make sure access requires a strong password and multifactor authentication. Do a household inventory. Make a list and take pictures of what you own. This can help if you have to file an insurance claim. Check out contractors before you need one. Ask people you know and trust for recommendations. Then search online for the company’s name with words like “scam” or “complaint.” Sign up for alerts and warnings in your area. Public safety officials use timely and reliable systems to alert you and your family in the event of severe weather and disasters. Plan for your pets. If you’re like millions nationwide, your pet is an important member of your household. A little planning today can help ensure safety for your pets during an emergency.

People have reported scammers covering up legit QR codes on parking meters with a QR code of their own. Protect your phone. Update your phone's operating system (OS) and apps to help prevent scammy links from turning into a hack: Apple Support: Update your iPhone or iPad Android Help: Check & update your Android version Use strong passwords for your accounts. Protect your online accounts with strong passwords and multi-factor authentication. Think you scanned a bad QR code? Follow these steps: Don’t interact with the scammer: If you reach out to someone through the website you think is fake, they may try to get money or sensitive information out of you. Change your password: If you entered credentials like your username or password, immediately change them wherever you use the same password for other accounts. Review your transactions: Check your credit card and bank statements to spot transactions you didn’t make. Then, report it to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. Image

content: While the car-buying process can be stressful, whether you’re shopping online or in person, the thought of driving off the dealer’s lot with that sweet ride you’ve had your eyes on can be exhilarating. But imagine showing up at the dealership and finding out the dealer has no record of your order or your payment. And that there’s no shiny car waiting for you! That’s what’s happening to unwitting car buyers who’ve been duped by scammers impersonating a car dealership. How the scam works Scammers set up bogus car dealership websites to trick you into paying up front for a car you’ll never lay hands on. They clone a real auto dealer’s website — often using AI to do so — copying the brand logos, vehicle listings, and photos down to the last detail. Some websites even include fake customer testimonials. They might advertise rare muscle cars or hard-to-find classics to lure you in. They describe the buying process in detail and offer flexible return policies to put you at ease. How to avoid the scam Here’s how to protect yourself from scammers that clone auto dealership websites. Search online for the dealer’s name with words like “scam,” “review,” or “complaint.” Any negative hits that come up are a red flag. Keep in mind that if the scammers are impersonating a real dealership, you might find glowing reviews. So go the extra mile — ask to see the car, and the dealership, in person. If they won’t let you, pump the brakes. If the car is too far for you to visit in person, tell the dealer you want to hire a mobile inspection service to check out the car. If they won’t let you, consider taking your business somewhere else. Report a scam Walk away if the dealer insists on an upfront payment by wire transfer only. And report them at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

Scammers know that and hope to steal money intended for disaster relief. Here’s what to know. To take advantage of your generosity, scammers might create fake charities that seem official. They claim to help people affected by weather emergencies or natural disasters. They also might impersonate well-known charity organizations, hoping that the familiar name will draw your donation. Either way, if you donate to these fakes, your money goes to the scammer, not the people in need. So how can you support impacted people without accidentally paying a scammer? Before you donate: Do some research. Search online for the cause you care about using terms like “hurricane relief” or “wildfire recovery.” If you get a request to donate to a cause on social media, research that, too. Don’t assume it’s legitimate because a friend posted it. Look charities up on Charity Watch or Give.org. See if it’s an established organization, not one that showed up overnight without a real way to help those in need. Also, find out exactly how much of your donation goes directly to the people the charity says it helps. Confirm the number. If someone asks you to donate by text, check the charity’s website first. Confirm you have the right number. Don’t donate to anyone who says you can only pay by cash, gift card, wiring money, or cryptocurrency. Legitimate charities will accept donations in many different ways. Learn more about donating safely at ftc.gov/charity. And if you spot a charity imposter, tell the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

content: Veterans across the country have reported getting postcards in the mail saying they (or their spouse) might qualify for extra monthly veterans benefits. But the “Veterans Savings Program” mentioned in the mailer doesn’t actually exist. It’s just a scammer phishing for personal or financial information. Here’s how this scam works so you can avoid it. Scammers often pretend to be affiliated with the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA). But in this new twist, scammers are mailing postcards to veterans, promising extra money through a “Veterans Savings Program.” (Remember: it’s not a real program.) The postcard might list the state you’re living in and mention real VA benefits like CHAMPVA or TRICARE For Life, hoping to seem more real. The message tells you to call right away or risk losing out. Scammers always hope you’ll act quickly rather than pause and do some research. Their goal is to trick you into calling and sharing personal information like your Social Security number or bank account details. If you get a postcard like this: Don’t respond. Legitimate VA communications will not pressure you to respond immediately or give sensitive information over the phone. Contact the VA directly if you have questions about your benefits. Always use a number you know is real — never the one in the postcard. Start with the VA Benefits Hotline at 1-800-827-1000. Spread the word. Scammers typically don’t just contact one person. Sharing this advice can help others in your community spot and avoid the scam. Sign up for email updates to get the latest on scams like this one at MilitaryConsumer.gov. If you spot this or another VA benefits scam, report it to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov and to the VA at VSAFE.gov or 1-833-38V-SAFE.

content: Did you get a package you didn’t order? It could be a brushing scam where a scammer uses your name to leave a fake review for that package you didn’t order. It could also be a sign that someone has (or is looking to steal) your personal information. It starts with an unexpected package that looks like it’s from a known company like Amazon, or from a person or business you’ve never heard of. The package is addressed to you and recent reports to the FTC say it usually has something cheap and random inside, like baby wipes, toothpaste, or seeds. Why would someone send you that? Scammers do this so they have “validation” of delivery. Then they use your name to place fake reviews online about their business to “brush up” their sales. Sometimes, the sender might leave a note with a QR code inside the package. It might say to scan to find out who sent the package, or to process a return. But scanning could take you to a phishing website designed to steal information like your credit card numbers, usernames, or passwords. If you got a package you didn’t order: Change passwords on all your online shopping accounts in case they were compromised. If the package came from Amazon or another online marketplace, message the platform so they can investigate removing the seller. Check your credit weekly for free at AnnualCreditReport.com. Monitor the information in your credit report and look for signs of identity theft. Know that the law says you don’t need to return things you didn’t order. And you don’t have to pay for them, either. But be cautious about using the product. After all, you don’t know who sent it. If you spot a brushing scam, tell the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

content: If you owe back taxes, there are ways to get real help. But dishonest companies will promise to get rid of your debt for “pennies on the dollar,” before even looking into your tax situation. They’ll often charge service fees without actually doing anything for you, and leave you further in the hole with local, state, or federal tax authorities. That’s exactly what led to the FTC’s nearly $10 million settlement with the owners of American Tax Service (ATS). According to the FTC, ATS mailed out letters impersonating the government, demanding that people call by a specific date or risk property seizure. The FTC also says ATS ran ads on TV, radio, and online, including on podcasts, which led people to scammy sales calls filled with false promises of tax debt resolution. If you need help paying your taxes: Ignore promises from businesses that say you "qualify" for a tax relief program or that they’ll settle your debt for only a fraction of what you owe. Only the IRS or your state’s comptroller or revenue department can decide what you qualify for. Don't do business with anyone that tells you to pay their whole fee upfront. If they say that, walk away. Know that no company can guarantee a particular result. Every taxpayer’s situation is unique. Visit the IRS’ Taxpayer Advocate Service website for help with federal tax problems you can’t resolve on your own. For help with state taxes, contact your state comptroller. And if you spot a scam, tell the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

content: You’re browsing your social media feed when an ad grabs your attention mid-swipe: that designer bag you’ve been dreaming of is 50% off for a limited time only! You’re dying to get your hands on one, so you don’t think twice about clicking on the ad. Why would you? The ad is right there in your feed and it looks real, so you trust that it’s legit. But it might not be. That’s because social media platforms don’t always thoroughly vet the ads you see or the advertisers behind them. Unfortunately, scammers are taking advantage of that, and some consumers are paying the price. According to an FTC data spotlight, in 2025, people reported losses of more than $95 million to scams that started when they ordered something after seeing an ad on social media. And since a lot of people don’t report scams, real losses are likely much higher. How to avoid fake or scammy ads on social media Because ads on social media aren’t always thoroughly vetted by platforms, it’s a good idea to check out the company before you buy based on an ad or post. Look online for its name plus “scam” or “complaint.” Anyone can pay to place ads in your social media feed — including scammers impersonating real brands, selling knock-off products, or touting a program to teach you how to invest and beat the stock market. And they can show you personalized ads based on your online activity like your interests and shopping habits. Check out What To Do About Online Tracking and Personalized Ads to learn how to review and adjust your privacy and advertising settings in your browser, phone, and apps. Report scams on social media If you spot or lose money to a fake or scammy ad, report it to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

content: Learn to trade online! Get rich! Quit your job! Social media is flooded with people flashing fancy cars and exotic trips, claiming you can have the same lifestyle just by “learning to trade.” But they rarely mention the truth: trading is risky, there are no guaranteed returns, and you can lose a lot of money fast. That’s what happened to the young people targeted on social media by International Markets Live (IML), also known as IM Mastery Academy and IYOVIA, according to a lawsuit brought by the Federal Trade Commission. The agency says IML advertised ”educators” who often had no legitimate credentials, and the FTC says, the company used false earning claims to recruit people into a large investment training scheme. Thanks to the agency’s action, the company is no longer in business, its leaders must turn over assets valued at over $90 million, and they’re banned from selling trading training services and investment opportunities in the future. If you’re considering a business opportunity or learning how to trade online here’s what to know and do: No one can guarantee you’ll make lots of money with little to no risk. Anyone who does is a scammer. No one can guarantee to teach you how to trade successfully in the financial markets. Anyone who does is a scammer. Research the company, its officials, and its promoters. Search online with their name plus words like “review,” “scam,” or “fraud.” Go through several pages of search results, since the first search results you see might be paid ads. Also, check with your state attorney general for complaints. Take your time and talk to someone you trust. Ask questions and get a second opinion about the coaching program from someone who has your best interests in mind. Spotted a scam? Report it at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

content: They’re the worst of the absolute worst: scams that target people who have already lost money to a scam. If you or someone you know paid a scammer, here’s what to know to avoid scammers who pretend to be helpers. Refund and recovery scammers buy lists of people who’ve already been scammed, hoping they can be scammed again. The scammers contact you, saying they’ll help get your money back or recover the prize or merchandise you never got. To sound trustworthy, they might say they’re with a government agency (even the FTC), a consumer advocacy group, or a law firm — but it’s all a lie. They’ll then tell you to pay a “retainer fee,” “processing fee,” or “administrative charge,” or share your financial information so they can (supposedly) deposit the refund. But if you pay, they’ll steal your money…and if you share your information, they might steal your identity. To avoid these scams: Don’t trust someone who contacts you claiming they can recover your lost money for a fee. You’ll lose more money. Never pay up front for a refund…or for help getting one. Neither government agencies nor legitimate organizations will ever ask for money or financial info in exchange for help getting a refund. Anyone who does is a scammer. Always research anyone who contacts you about a refund. Search online for their name plus words like “complaint,” “scam,” or “review.” Look up the contact info for government agencies on your own, if you want to confirm they contacted you. content: Scammers know that applying for veterans benefits is at the top of the to-do list when you’re getting ready to leave the military. That’s why they pretend to be with the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) and offer to help you apply for benefits if you pay them — even though it’s free to apply with the VA. So if you’re applying for veterans benefits, get the help you need while avoiding scams. Here’s how. First, know how the scam works: You get an unexpected call, text, email, or message on social media from someone who says they’re reaching out about your veterans benefits. They might claim to work for the VA or say they’re “approved” by the VA. (But, really, they’re not.) They offer to help you do things like apply for benefits you’re “missing,” get you a 100% disability rating, or speed up the claims process — all for a fee. Those are all scams. The VA will never charge you to apply for benefits. Accredited representatives and recognized Veterans Service Organizations (VSOs) won’t charge you either, but scammers will. A few things to remember: Never pay to apply. Whether you apply online or in person at a VA Regional Office, the VA will help you gather and develop evidence to support your initial claim for VA benefits — for free. Apply directly to the VA. Only the VA can determine your eligibility and award benefits. Anything else is a scam. Only scammers guarantee you’ll get benefits or offer to help you skip the line. Not even accredited representatives can do that. Work with a VA accredited representative. Use the VA’s Accreditation Search tool to make sure that the person helping you is actually approved by the VA. If you spot a VA impersonation scam, tell the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. Then, tell your state attorney general.

content: Whether you’ve been planning a move for months or you’re dealing with last-minute orders, military moves can be both exciting and stressful. The last thing you need is a rental scam to raise that stress level, so here’s how to spot them. Some scammers make up listings for housing that’s not for rent or doesn’t exist. Others steal pictures from legit listings. They post their fake listings on a different site and grab your attention with below market rent. And since they can’t get into the property (it’s not theirs to rent), they make up excuses for why you can’t see it in person, which could be a sign of a scam. Another sign of a scam is a “landlord” who says you can only pay for a rental with cash, a gift card, cryptocurrency, or a wire transfer service. If you pay, the scammer will disappear with your money — and you’ll be left with no place to move to. Even if you’re rushing to secure a new address, slow down. Before you sign or pay for an apartment, do some recon: Search the rental address online. If you find the same property listed with a different price or landlord, it’s likely a scam. Check it out in person if you can. If you’re not local, ask someone you trust to go on a tour of the home for you — or to drive by to make sure the home they see matches what you saw advertised. The relocation or housing referral office at your new base can also help with finding places to rent (and companies to avoid). Pay attention to how they ask you to pay. Paying for a rental with a gift card or cryptocurrency or through a wire transfer service like Western Union or MoneyGram is like sending cash. After you send the money, it’s hard to get it back. Report rental listing scams to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov and your state’s attorney general.

content: We’ve written about this scam before, but like a bad sequel, it’s back. People are telling the FTC they’ve gotten letters in the mail from law firms about unclaimed life insurance money. Have you gotten one of these? The “lawyer” says that one of their clients, with your same last name, died and you’re the heir to a life insurance policy worth millions. (Spoiler alert: you’re not.) The letter then explains that they’d like to split the proceeds between you, some charity organizations, and their law firm. But what’s really happening here? Here’s the first thing to know: this is not a letter from a lawyer — it’s from a scammer. The letter might sound convincing, with the firm supposedly trying to contact family members and finding no heir to “the fortune.” You might even be tempted to reply, since maybe the worst that happens is you don’t get a share of the money. But there is worse: if you contact them, they’ll try to get your personal and financial information (like your Social Security or bank account numbers), your money, or all of the above. And that life insurance policy or inheritance? It doesn’t exist at all. Here’s what to do if you get one of these letters: Don’t respond. Keep your money and information to yourself. Never send money or information to a stranger who promises big rewards. That’s always a scam. Pass this information on to a friend. You probably throw away these kinds of letters, but you probably know someone who could use a friendly reminder that these are scams. Report it to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. content: Scammers promise to solve your debt problems to trick you into paying them instead of your actual lender. If a caller offers to help you enroll in a special “military debt forgiveness” program, pause. That’s probably a scam. Learn how debt relief scammers might target the military and how to avoid the scam. Scammy debt relief companies call out of the blue and use official-sounding names and phrases to suggest ties to the military. They might claim to be from a military bank or credit union, like USAA or Navy Federal, or a credit bureau like Equifax, Experian, or Transunion. But if the caller offers to help you reduce or settle your debt — after you pay a fee — that’s a sure sign of a scam. It’s illegal for a debt relief company to charge you before they help you. Some companies offer to enroll you in “exclusive” military debt relief or veteran debt forgiveness programs, but those programs might not even exist. If you pay upfront, you might lose your money and get nothing in return. Some scammers pressure you to pay them instead of your real creditors. But missing payments on your real debt can lower your credit score and mess up things like your security clearance. You could end up using your hard-earned savings to pay down the increased debt plus late fees and penalties. Need help managing debt? Start by contacting your lender directly. Ask about your repayment options. To avoid a debt relief scam: Never pay upfront for debt relief. Only scammers try to collect fees from you before they settle any of your debts. Find help. Financial counseling resources for active duty are available through an on-base personal financial manager or counselor. If you’re a veteran, find help through the VA Do some research. But it’s all a lie. If someone says the only way to pay for your pet’s treatment is with a gift card, a payment app, cryptocurrency, or a wire transfer service, you’re dealing with a scammer. Scammers impersonate real animal shelters and hospitals collecting donations for pets in need. They might create fake webpages and posts using stolen or AI-generated images of pets in need of forever homes. If someone asks you to donate, check ftc.gov/charity for advice on how to donate safely. And, as part of your research, do a reverse image search to see if the images are stolen. Scammers want you to think you won a prize because you previously donated to help animals. The name of the prize or organization might sound real but it’s another lie. If you have to pay to collect a prize or sweepstakes winnings, you know it’s a scam. Don’t let scammers rush you into making a decision. Slow down and talk to someone you trust. And if you spot one of these scams, tell the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

content: As summer approaches, your kids might be looking for downtime (and screen time). To keep them safe while they’re spending time online, start with a conversation about your family’s rules and expectations — then consider setting parental controls to help. Parental controls can help you limit the types of content your kids can access, how much time they spend online, and who they can chat with. As you consider parental controls, you may want to think about which settings and functions might be most helpful: What shows and movies are your kids watching? TV and movie ratings suggest what content might be appropriate based on your child’s age — and help you decide which ratings should be blocked. What online games are your kids playing? Ratings and reviews for video games can help you decide if they’re okay for your kids. How do your kids stay connected with friends? Many gaming and social media apps with chat functions have settings parents can use to approve a list of friends, or prevent online communication altogether, which helps keep kids from chatting with strangers. Ready to set up parental controls on your kids’ apps and devices? Start with free tools like Apple’s Family Sharing, Google’s Family Link, and Microsoft Family Safety to set screen time limits, restrict apps and content, and get information about your kid’s website and app activity. Check settings on video games and cell phones. Is your kid a gamer? Check out controls for gaming platforms, apps, and websites. If your kids have cell phones or connected watches, look for privacy and security settings to block your kids from sharing their location with people they don’t know. Add passcodes or PINs to shared devices — or create separate profiles. That way no one can stream shows and movies, scroll social media apps, or make purchases under your account without your permission. content: Summer is here! If you haven't made your vacation plans yet, you might be looking for a deal. While you look for bargains, scammers are looking for ways to reach you…and your money. Here are some things to know to help you avoid travel scams. Travel scams can crop up when you’re searching online for hotels or flights. Scammers sometimes use paid ads and put their number alongside a well-known company’s name, or link to a website that only looks like it belongs to a hotel brand or airline. To avoid these scammers, scroll to the unpaid search results and check that you have the right website or contact info for the business you’re looking for. Or better yet, type the company’s website directly into the browser, if you know it. Scammers have driving vacations covered, too, sending texts about fake “ unpaid tolls ” and demanding immediate payment. If you’re not sure that text is real, reach out to the state’s toll agency using a phone number or website you know is right — not the info from the text. Here are some other ways to avoid travel scams: Get all the details of a travel offer before you commit. If the organizer can’t or won’t give you more specific details (other than saying “you’ll stay at a ‘five-star’ resort”), walk away. Do some research. Look up the names of travel companies, hotels, rentals, and agents with the words “scam,” “review,” or “complaint.” See what others say about them before you commit. Look at how they ask you to pay. Only scammers say the only way to pay is by wire transfer, gift card, payment app, or cryptocurrency. They prefer these methods because, once they’ve collected the money, it’s almost impossible to get it back. Learn more at ftc.gov/TravelScams. Spot a scam? Tell the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

content: Today is World Elder Abuse Awareness Day (WEAAD). WEAAD gives all of us a chance to raise awareness about elder financial abuse, neglect, and exploitation. An issue that continues to impact the wellbeing of people of all ages — including older adults — is scams. In 2025, people reported losing about $16 billion to scams, compared to $12.8 billion the previous year. And because not everyone who experiences a scam reports it, this likely represents only a fraction of the actual amount lost. This year, the FTC is joining other government agencies, businesses, and organizations across the country to help raise awareness about the top reported scam: imposters. These scammers pretend to be someone they’re not — like someone from a government agency or well-known business — to trick you into giving them money or your personal information. How can you help spread the word about imposters? Use the “Never Ever” campaign toolkit at ejcc.acl.gov, which has information and resources to help your friends, family, and community recognize, avoid, and report imposter scams. And know that: Never ever will someone from the government say: “Your money isn’t safe. Move it to protect it.” Only a scammer will. Never ever will someone from the government threaten to suspend your government benefits if you don’t pay immediately. Only a scammer will. Never ever will someone from the government demand that you pay with a payment app, cryptocurrency, wire transfers, or gift cards. Find more at ejcc.acl.gov. Use the campaign’s hashtags, #StopGovImposters and #StopBizImposters, to share what you know with others. And if you spot an imposter scam (or any other type of scam), report it at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

content: Did you get a call claiming you missed jury duty and need to pay? Followed by a text or email with official-looking documents saying there’s a warrant out for your arrest? As alarming as these things sound, they’re a scam designed to steal your money. Most jury duty scams start with an “urgent” call from someone claiming to be a U.S. Marshal or an officer from your local police department. To catch you off guard, the caller might already know things about you, like your full name or address. They say you missed jury duty (you didn’t) and threaten to arrest you (they won’t) unless you pay a fine using a payment app or cryptocurrency. That scam is probably familiar so far, but now scammers also text or email you a document that looks like an official warrant for your arrest, complete with how much you owe for missing jury duty. While this might make the scam look more convincing, it’s all fake. Here’s how you know it’s a scam: Real law enforcement will never text or email you an arrest warrant. Even if the caller ID looks like it’s coming from your local police department or the U.S. Marshals, real law enforcement officers won’t call to say they’ll arrest you. And they won’t threaten to arrest you if you hang up. Courts never demand payment over the phone. In fact, no government agency will. Only scammers say you can only pay with a payment app, cryptocurrency, gift cards, or a wire transfer service like Western Union or MoneyGram. If you get a call like this, tell the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. And if you already paid a scammer, read What To Do if You Were Scammed to find out what to do next.

content: When you search online, do you click the first result you see? You’re not alone. But that habit could cost you — especially if you’re searching for health insurance or government healthcare programs like Medicare. Sometimes dishonest businesses pay to place ads at the top of search results that look like official government websites. They’re designed to trick you into sharing personal information, paying unnecessary fees, or signing up for misleading services. That’s why you might want to view more than just the top search results. Here’s what it can look like when you’re dealing with an impersonator, from a case the FTC settled with MediaAlpha: You search for “aca insurance”: Image You get this list of websites: Image You click on the first one: Image But that takes you to an impersonator, not the real government agency: Image So what can you do to avoid a search scam? Spot the “Ad”: Always look for a small “Ad” or “Sponsored” label next to the search result. These labels mean someone paid for that placement. Check the URL: When a site’s address ends with.gov, it’s from the U.S. government. Most government websites end in.gov (like HealthCare.gov), so a web address ending in.com,.org, or something else could be a sign you’re dealing with someone else. Scroll Down: The organic search results below the paid ads are ranked by relevance, not by who paid the most, so they may be more likely to get you to the right place. The bottom line: Take an extra second to scroll. Make sure you’re getting real information from the real source, not a scammer’s lookalike. And if you see a search scam? Tell the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.
